comparator.name: Future Planet Studies
comparator.sourceNotes: The current official UvA curriculum defines a 180-EC programme with 60 EC in each year. Year 1 is a compulsory shared programme in climate and energy, quality of life, Earth and social systems, environmental economics, hazards, data and research. In Year 2 every student follows 15 EC of shared philosophy, scenario-planning and food-forestry study plus one 45-EC major. The normalized target is the generic bachelor; Future Earth and Future Society are equally formal specialisations, and neither is identified as the general route. Future Earth is therefore selected by its first-listed position in the current official curriculum, independently of UCR fit. Its 45 EC combines Earth science, biology and chemistry through plant-soil study, food and ecosystems, remote sensing, R programming, statistics, digital Earth, aquatic systems, water management and desertification fieldwork. Year 3 preserves 30 EC of genuine open choice, followed by the 6-EC Future Planet Project, 6-EC Research Designs and an 18-EC major-specific Bachelor Project. The official February 2026 curriculum chart confirms these components and credits for 2026-2027.

alternativeSelection.assessment: After the closest Future Earth-informed programme, the official Future Society major supports a distinct governance-and-justice alternative, and the explicit energy-transition, green-building and environmental-enterprise evidence supports a third programme. All three are coherent, feasible and exceed the 30-EC pairwise course-difference floor, so the maximum of three UCR alternatives is reached.

comparisonAlignment.rationale: Both introduce complex sustainability challenges and systems thinking; the UvA course includes a first academic paper.
Both introduce geological, chemical and biological Earth-system processes.
Both examine climate-system processes, impacts, sea-level change and societal responses.
Both address ecosystems and biodiversity; the UvA course connects global biomes explicitly to food supply.
Both analyse spatial patterns of environmental hazards and adaptation; the UvA course uses Google Earth Pro.
Both develop remote-sensing and spatial-data methods for environmental change.
Both study soil properties and their environmental significance; the UvA course focuses specifically on plant-soil relations in food systems.
Both critically examine sustainable alternatives to industrial agriculture.
Both study water availability, hydrological processes, management and adaptation.
The compulsory Future Earth laboratory and field practical has no single ordinary UCR equivalent.
The dedicated aquatic-science and aquatic-ecosystem course has no single ordinary UCR equivalent.
The preparatory environmental-data course tied to the Desertification field course has no separate UCR equivalent.
The dedicated field course in geo-ecological mapping and desertification has no single ordinary UCR equivalent.
Both develop future-oriented responses to coupled human-environment problems; the UvA course teaches formal complexity-based scenario planning.
Both examine how science, politics, institutions and society shape sustainability transitions.
Both examine human-nature conflict and environmental justice; the UvA course frames these questions through quality of life.
Both introduce economic systems, environmental externalities and responses to environmental problems.
Both compare energy sources and transitions through technical, economic and environmental perspectives.
Both teach research design and quantitative methods; the UvA course directly scaffolds the parallel Bachelor Project.
Both introduce data processing, visualisation and statistical analysis for applied research.
Both develop statistical models, uncertainty estimation and hypothesis testing.
Both are collaborative sustainability research projects addressing complex real-world environmental problems.
The dedicated group research course combining interviews and surveys around quality of life has no single ordinary UCR equivalent.
The compulsory programme-specific philosophy-of-science course has no single course in these UCR schedules.
The dedicated R programming course has no separate ordinary-course equivalent in these UCR schedules.
The genuine 30-EC elective semester remains student-selected and is not a fixed external course to align.
The compulsory 18-EC individual Bachelor Project cannot be counted as an ordinary UCR course or as UCR's optional comparison-only research element.

notes.text: UvA organises Future Planet Studies around semester challenges, a formal 45-EC Future Earth major, dedicated R and spatial-methods courses, field and laboratory practicals, and an 18-EC Bachelor Project. UCR can construct coherent programmes across the same broad environmental and societal territory, but it distributes that study across separate courses rather than reproducing UvA's integrated challenge sequence and major structure.
